questions.question: State the consruction of reley.
questions.solution_html:
• State the construction of relay. /
  • Ans: A relay is an important electromechanical device used in electrical and electronic circuits for
  • controlling high power or high voltage circuits with the help of a small control signal. The
  • construction of a relay is quite simple but very effective. At the heart of a relay lies an electromagnet,
  • which is basically a coil of insulated copper wire wound around a soft iron core. Along with this, there
  • is an armature, which is a movable soft iron piece connected to a spring. The armature is placed
  • close to the electromagnet in such a way that when the coil is energized, the magnetic field pulls the
  • armature towards the core. The armature is mechanically linked with a set of contacts. These
  • contacts are of two types—normally open (NO) and normally closed (NC). A base frame holds all
  • these parts together, and the spring helps the armature return to its original position when the coil is
  • de-energized.
questions.source_exam: First Semester MGU-UGP/MGU-BBA/MGU-BCA Honours Examinations November 2025
questions.final_answer: de-energized.

questions.question: List the different types of switches and explain toggle switch.
questions.solution_html:
• List the different types of switches and explain toggle switch. /
  • Ans: Types of switches ; Slide Switch, toggle switch, push to, on switch and push to off switch.
  • A toggle switch is one of the most common types of electrical switches used to control the flow of
  • current in a circuit. It operates through a simple mechanism where a lever, handle, or knob is flipped
  • back and forth to make or break an electrical connection. The name “toggle” comes from the
  • mechanical action of moving the lever between two stable positions, usually ON and OFF. This simple
  • yet reliable design has made toggle switches highly popular in a wide variety of electrical and electronic
  • applications. Structurally, a toggle switch consists of a lever connected to an internal set of electrical
  • contacts. When the lever is pushed in one direction, the contacts close and allow current to pass
  • through, whereas when the lever is pushed in the opposite direction, the contacts open and stop the
  • flow of electricity. Depending on the requirement, toggle switc hes can be single -pole single-throw
  • (SPST), single-pole double - throw (SPDT), double -pole single-throw (DPST), or double -pole double -
  • throw (DPDT). This variety allows them to be used for simple ON/OFF control as well as for more
  • complex switching operations like reversing the direction of a motor or selecting between two different
  • circuits. One of the key advantages of toggle switches is their durability and ease of use. The firm
  • clicking action when the lever is flipped provides tactile feedback, making them convenient to operate
  • even without looking. They are also capable of handling a wide range of voltages and currents, which
  • makes them suitable for both low -power electronic devices and heavy -duty electrical equipment.
  • Moreover, toggle switches are available in different sizes, mounting styles, and designs, making them
  • adaptable to various applications in industries, homes, and vehicles. From a practical standpoint,
  • toggle switches are essential in daily life because they provide a simple, mechanical, and reliable
  • means of controlling electricity. Their visible ON/OFF positions also make them safe and easy to
  • identify, reducing the risk of accidental misuse.

questions.question: Explain the application of LCR circuits in resonance experiments and power factor improvement.
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the application of LCR circuits in resonance experiments and power factor improvement.
  • /
  • Ans: LCR circuits (containing an inductor L, capacitor C, and resistor R) are widely used in resonance
  • experiments because they show a sharp rise in current at the resonant frequency. At resonance, the
  • inductive reactance and capacitive reactance cancel each other, making the circuit purely resistive.
  • This principle is used in radio receivers, communication systems, and frequency-selective filters to
  • select a particular frequency from many incoming signals.
  • LCR circuits are also useful in improving the power factor of electrical systems. Industrial loads often
  • have low power factor due to inductive machines. By connecting an LCR circuit—usually a capacitor
  • in series or parallel with the load—the reactive power is reduced and the circuit becomes closer to
  • resistive. This improves the power factor, reduces losses, and increases the efficiency of power
  • transmission.
questions.source_exam: First Semester MGU-UGP/MGU-BBA/MGU-BCA Honours Examinations November 2025
questions.final_answer: transmission.

questions.question: Explain the working of a Zener diode as a voltage regulator.
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the working of a Zener diode as a voltage regulator . /
  • Ans: A Zener diode is a special type of diode that is mainly designed to work in the reverse bias
  • condition. In an ordinary diode, when reverse voltage increases beyond a certain limit, the diode
  • breaks down permanently and gets damaged. But in a Zener diode, the diode is specially made
  • so that it can safely undergo this breakdown without getting destroyed. This safe breakdown is
  • known as Zener breakdown.
  • The most important feature of a Zener diode is that it maintains a constant voltage across it,
  • even if the current flowing through it changes. Because of this property, it is widely used as a
  • voltage regulator in electronic circuits. The voltage at which the Zener diode breaks down and
  • starts conducting in reverse bias is called the Zener voltage. This voltage is a fixed value, and it
  • is carefully set during the manufacturing process. For example, a 5.6V Zener diode will always
  • maintain about 5.6V across it once it enters breakdown. To understand its working, imagine a circuit
  • where the Zener diode is connected in reverse across a power supply. As the supply voltage
  • increases, initially the diode does not conduct much current. But once the supply reaches the Zener
  • voltage, the diode suddenly allows current to flow in reverse. At the same time, the voltage across
  • the diode does not increase further; it stays nearly constant at the Zener voltage. In this way, the
  • Zener diode protects sensitive components in the circuit from high voltages and ensures that they
  • always receive a stable supply.
  • The operation of the Zener diode is based on two mechanisms: Zener breakdown and
  • avalanche breakdown. Zener breakdown happens at low reverse voltages, where the electric
  • field is strong enough to pull electrons from their atomic bonds. Avalanche breakdown happens
  • at higher voltages, where carriers gain enough energy to knock out more electrons and create a
  • chain reaction. In both cases, the diode can conduct in reverse safely, but without being
  • damaged.
  • Zener diodes are manufactured in different voltage ratings, from a few volts up to several
  • hundred volts. They are usually made from silicon because silicon provides better performance
  • and stability. When used in circuits, a small resistor is generally connected in series with the
  • Zener diode. This resistor limits the current flowing through the diode and prevents it from
  • overheating. In practice, Zener diodes are commonly used for voltage regulation in power supplies,
  • protection of circuits from over-voltage, waveform shaping, and reference voltage generation.
  • For example, in a power supply circuit, if we use a 12V Zener diode, then no matter how much
  • the input supply fluctuates above 12V, the output will remain fixed at 12V . This makes Zener
  • diodes very important in designing stable electronic systems. Thus, the Zener diode is not just a
  • normal diode but a specially designed component that takes advantage of controlled reverse
  • breakdown. Its ability to maintain constant voltage makes it one of the simplest and most
  • effective devices for regulation and protection in electronics.
questions.source_exam: First Semester MGU-UGP/MGU-BBA/MGU-BCA Honours Examinations November 2025
questions.final_answer: effective devices for regulation and protection in electronics.

questions.question: Define a rocker switch and state its construction and working principle with a neat diagram
questions.solution_html:
• Define a rocker switch and state its construction and working principle with a neat diagram.
  • /
  • Ans: A rocker switch is an electromechanical switching device that operates by rocking a
  • movable actuator back and forth to open or close an electrical circuit. It is widely used in
  • household appliances, power supplies, automotive dashboards and control panels because
  • it provides a simple ON/OFF action with clear visual and tactile feedback. When one side of
  • the actuator is pressed, the switch rocks into the ON position and completes the circuit;
  • when the opposite side is pressed, it rocks back to the OFF position and breaks the circuit.
  • This rocking motion gives the switch its name and makes it easy to operate even without
  • looking at it.
  • In terms of construction, a rocker switch consists of a moulded insulating housing that
  • encloses all the electrical and mechanical components. The upper part of the device is the
  • rocker or actuator, which is shaped like a small curved plate that pivots around a central
  • fulcrum. Inside the switch, a small spring mechanism is provided to give a firm snap action
  • and to hold the switch reliably in either the ON or OFF position. Beneath the actuator lie the
  • metallic contacts. These include one or more fixed contacts connected to the external
  • terminals and a moving contact that is attached to the rocker mechanism. When the
  • actuator is rocked, the moving contact either touches the fixed contacts to complete the
  • circuit, or lifts away to open the circuit. The terminals at the bottom of the switch allow it to
  • be connected to external wiring, typically in SPST or SPDT configurations. The entire
  • assembly is compact, insulated and designed to withstand repeated mechanical operation.
  • The working principle of a rocker switch is based purely on mechanical contact-making and
  • breaking. When the user presses the rocker on the ON side, the actuator pivots around its
  • hinge and pushes the moving contact into the fixed contacts. This closes the circuit and
  • allows the current to flow. The spring provides stability so that the switch remains in this
  • position until it is manually pressed again. Pressing the opposite side of the rocker causes
  • the actuator to reverse its position, and the moving contact is pulled away from the fixed
  • contacts, thereby interrupting the current flow and switching the device OFF. Some rocker
  • switches include an internal indicator lamp or LED that glows when the circuit is closed,
  • making it easy to identify the switch state.

questions.question: Write short notes on practical applications of series and parallel LCR circuits, including Q-factor and power factor.
questions.solution_html:
• Write short notes on practical applications of series and parallel LCR circuits, including Q-factor
  • and power factor . /
  • Ans: Series and parallel LCR circuits play an important role in many practical electronic and
  • electrical applications because of their ability to control impedance, resonance, selectivity,
  • and phase relationships between voltage and current. A series LCR circuit combines an
  • inductor, capacitor and resistor in a single path. When such a circuit is driven by an AC
  • source, it exhibits a sharp resonance at the frequency where the inductive reactance equals
  • the capacitive reactance. At this resonant condition, the impedance of the circuit becomes
  • minimum and the current reaches a maximum value. This property makes series LCR circuits
  • extremely useful in applications such as radio tuning circuits, signal selection in
  • communication receivers, induction heating, and audio frequency filtering. The circuit’s Q-
  • factor, defined as the ratio of reactive power to real power at resonance, determines the
  • sharpness of resonance. A high Q-factor indicates high selectivity, meaning that the circuit
  • can isolate a narrow band of frequencies, which is essential in radio broadcast receivers and
  • selective amplifiers.
  • A parallel LCR circuit, on the other hand, consists of the resistor, inductor and capacitor
  • connected in parallel across an AC supply. Instead of minimizing impedance at resonance
  • like the series circuit, the parallel arrangement produces a condition where the total current
  • drawn from the source becomes minimum at the resonant frequency. The circuit impedance
  • is maximum at resonance, and most of the current circulates between the inductor and
  • capacitor branches. This makes parallel LCR circuits suitable for applications like tank circuits
  • in oscillators, impedance matching networks, and filter networks where stable frequency
  • operation and high impedance are required. The Q-factor of a parallel LCR circuit also
  • influences the stability and purity of oscillations produced in LC oscillators and RF
  • transmitters, as a higher Q ensures a narrower bandwidth and better frequency stability.
  • In both types of circuits, the power factor plays a significant role in determining energy
  • efficiency. Power factor is the cosine of the phase angle between the supply voltage and the
  • current. In LCR circuits, the presence of inductive and capacitive reactance causes the
  • current to lead or lag the voltage depending on which reactance dominates. At resonance,
  • the power factor becomes unity because the net reactance is zero and the voltage and
  • current are in phase. This condition is desirable in many power applications since it ensures
  • maximum power transfer and minimum losses. Improving power factor in practical systems,
  • such as transmission lines and industrial loads, often involves using LCR combinations to
  • balance reactive power.
  • Thus, series and parallel LCR circuits find extensive use in tuning, filtering, signal processing,
  • oscillation generation, and power management. Their behaviour, governed by resonance, Q-
  • factor and power factor, makes them indispensable components in both communication
  • electronics and power engineering applications.

questions.question: Model a simple circuit and show how the maximum power transfer theorem is applied to find maximum power delivered to a load.
questions.solution_html:
• Model a simple circuit and show how the maximum power transfer theorem is applied to find
  • maximum power delivered to a load. /
  • Ans: The maximum power transfer theorem says that a load receives maximum power from a
  • network when the load resistance (RL) is equal to the internal resistance (Rth) of the
  • source.
  • In very simple words:
  • “A load gets maximum power when RL = Rth.”
  • Step 1 — Find 𝑉𝑡ℎ(open-circuit voltage at the load terminals):
  • Remove 𝑅𝑜(open circuit). Then no current flows in the 25Ωbranch, so the top junction left of the
  • 25Ω(call it node A) is determined only by the 10Ωand the 40Ωto ground:
  • 𝑉𝐴 = 30 ⋅ 4010 + 40 = 30 ⋅ 4050 = 30 ⋅ 0.8 = 24 V.
  • With no current through 25Ωthe drop across it is zero, so the open terminal (node B) is at the same
  • potential:
  • 𝑉𝑡ℎ = 𝑉𝐵 = 24 V.
  • Step 2 — Find 𝑅𝑡ℎ(with source turned off):
  • Short the 30 V source. Node A then has two resistances to ground: 10Ω(shorted source side) and
  • 40Ω— these are in parallel:
  • 𝑅𝐴→𝑔 = 10 ∥ 40 = 10 ⋅ 4010 + 40 = 40050 = 8 Ω.
  • Looking into the open terminals (node B to ground) you see the 25Ωin series with that parallel
  • combination, so
  • 𝑅𝑡ℎ = 25 + 8 = 33 Ω.
  • Step 3 — Maximum power delivered to the load:
  • Maximum power occurs when 𝑅𝐿 = 𝑅𝑡ℎ = 33 Ω
  • 𝑃max = 𝑉𝑡ℎ24𝑅𝑡ℎ = 2424 ⋅ 33 = 576132 ≈ 4.36 W.
  • • 𝑉𝑡ℎ = 24 V
  • • 𝑅𝑡ℎ = 33 Ω
  • • Optimum load 𝑅𝐿 = 33 for maximum power
  • • 𝑃max ≈ 4.36 W

questions.question: Explain what valence electrons are and describe how they help in forming bonds between atoms.
questions.solution_html:
• Explain what valence electrons are and describe how they help in forming bonds between atoms.
  • /
  • Ans: Every atom in the universe is made up of three main particles — protons, neutrons, and
  • electrons. Protons and neutrons stay inside the center of the atom called the nucleus, while
  • electrons move around the nucleus in different circular paths known as shells or energy levels.
  • These shells are named as K, L, M, N, and so on. Each shell can hold a certain number of
  • electrons.Among all these electrons, the ones that are present in the outermost shell of an atom
  • are called valence electrons. These electrons play a very important role in deciding how an
  • atom will behave or react with other atoms. In simple words, valence electrons are responsible
  • for forming bonds between atoms.
  • For example, if we take a sodium atom, it has one electron in its outermost shell. That means it
  • has one valence electron. Similarly, chlorine has seven electrons in its outermost shell. Sodium
  • wants to lose one electron to become stable, and chlorine wants to gain one electron to
  • complete its shell. When they come together, sodium gives its one valence electron to chlorine,
  • and both become stable. This forms a compound called sodium chloride (NaCl) — which is
  • nothing but common salt.
  • This shows that valence electrons decide whether an atom will give or take electrons and how it
  • will combine with other atoms. If an atom has one, two, or three valence electrons, it usually
  • tries to lose them. If it has five, six, or seven valence electrons, it usually tries to gain electrons.
  • Atoms having eight valence electrons (like noble gases) are already stable and do not easily
  • react with other elements.
  • Valence electrons also determine many other properties of an element, such as whether it is a
  • metal, non-metal, or semiconductor . In metals, valence electrons are loosely bound to the
  • nucleus and can move freely, which makes metals good conductors of electricity. In non-metals,
  • valence electrons are tightly held, so they do not allow current to pass easily.
  • Valence electrons are the outermost electrons of an atom that decide its chemical behavior,
  • bonding nature, and electrical properties. Without understanding valence electrons, we cannot
  • explain why elements form compounds or how materials conduct electricity. They are the key to
  • understanding the entire chemistry of atoms and the formation of all substances around us.
  • x2 = 20]
